HarnessBandit: Joint Learnability–Transferability Scheduling
for Multi-Harness Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Hongliang Wei Affiliation:  Harbin Institute of Technology Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Xiaobing Tu Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Yinggui Wang Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Zhengxi Liu Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Rongkun Xue Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Jinkui Ren Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Xiantao Zhang Affiliation:  Alibaba Cloud* Equal contribution.† Corresponding authors.    Debin Zhao Affiliation:  Harbin Institute of Technology    Xiaopeng Fan Affiliation:  Harbin Institute of Technology
Abstract

Language-model agents are increasingly deployed through diverse harnesses that differ in system prompts, tool schemas, control loops, and trajectory formats. The same model can perform unevenly across these interfaces, making robustness to harness variation an important objective. A natural approach is to train a shared policy through multiple harnesses, but doing so introduces a scheduling problem: each training step should favor a harness that currently provides a useful learning signal while also producing an update that benefits the other harnesses. We develop HarnessBandit, an online scheduler that selects one harness per optimizer step. After a group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) update, it observes learnability—the mean absolute advantage on the batch—and transferability—the cosine between a low-dimensional gradient sketch of the current harness and exponential moving averages of the remaining harnesses. The two signals are fused after pooled sliding-window min–max normalization and sampled with a visit-dependent bonus and an explicit exploration floor. We train Qwen3.5-2B across six harnesses on ClawGym and evaluate on PinchBench (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness). HarnessBandit improves over mixed-batch multi-harness training on both benchmarks, while training diagnostics indicate that learnability and transferability provide distinct, evolving signals.

1 Introduction

Language-model agents interact with tools through a harness: a combination of system prompt, tool schema, planner or loop policy, and session bookkeeping that turns a user query into a trajectory of completions and tool calls (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Different harnesses induce different trajectory distributions even when the underlying task and reward function are held fixed. As a result, a policy trained exclusively through one interface need not transfer to another. Training with multiple harnesses can reduce this sensitivity, but requires deciding how their data should be allocated within and across optimizer steps.

This decision is not a standard multi-task mixture problem. The same ClawGym task can be executed under OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini CLI, or another scaffold; the task identity is shared, while the execution channel changes. We consider two properties of that channel. First, a batch is useful only if it produces a non-degenerate learning signal. Under group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025), a prompt group whose sampled trajectories receive identical rewards yields advantages near zero and therefore almost no policy gradient. We call this learnability. Second, an update computed on one harness may align with directions that other harnesses also require, or it may overfit one scaffold. We call the former cross-harness transferability. A static allocation of training steps responds to neither quantity.

We formulate multi-harness training as a non-stationary multi-armed bandit problem, where each harness is an arm and its online utility jointly reflects learnability and cross-harness transferability. We introduce HarnessBandit, a scheduling layer on top of GRPO rather than a new policy objective. At each step it selects one harness for a pure rollout batch, measures how much learning signal the batch provides and how well its update aligns with the other harnesses, and combines these observations to adapt the subsequent sampling distribution while retaining exploration.

We train a Qwen3.5-2B policy (Qwen Team, 2026) with Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) on 2,000 ClawGym tasks (RUC-AIBOX, 2025) crossed with six harnesses (12,000 prompt rows), and evaluate on PinchBench (held-out tasks under OpenClaw, an in-distribution harness) and ClawEval (held-out tasks under ClawEval’s native loop, an out-of-distribution harness). HarnessBandit obtains a PinchBench mean of 0.5060.506, compared with 0.4930.493 for a two-harness OpenClaw–Codex mixture and 0.3310.331 for a six-harness mixture (untuned base 0.3300.330). On ClawEval (161 tasks, N=3N{=}3), it reaches 41.6%41.6\% pass@3 and mean score 0.5560.556, compared with 38.5%38.5\% / 0.5100.510 and 29.8%29.8\% / 0.4900.490; Pass3 is 26.7%26.7\%, matching the base model and above both mixtures.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    We formulate multi-harness training as a non-stationary bandit over execution interfaces, rather than as a fixed mixture over tasks or domains.

  2. 2.

    We propose two complementary trainer-native signals—local learnability and cross-harness transferability—and combine them so the scheduler prefers updates that are both informative and aligned with other interfaces.

  3. 3.

    We conduct experiments on PinchBench (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw) and ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness), where HarnessBandit improves over static harness mixtures under a matched GRPO budget without collapsing to a single arm.

2 Related work

Agentic reinforcement learning and tool use.

Tool-using language agents interleave reasoning with environment actions (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024). Subsequent work has treated the agent–computer interface itself as a first-class design object: SWE-agent showed that scaffolding choices change success rates on software-engineering tasks (Yang et al., 2024), OpenHands and SWE-Gym provide open stacks for training and evaluating such agents (Wang et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2024), and web and personal-assistant benchmarks stress long-horizon tool use (Zhou et al., 2024; Yao and others, 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Reinforcement learning has been applied to reasoning traces (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Yu et al., 2025) and, more recently, to agent trajectories with programmatic rewards. Polar (Xu et al., 2026) exposes multiple harnesses as interchangeable rollout backends behind a shared trainer. We use that interface. Our question is orthogonal to the choice of policy gradient: given several harnesses, which one should generate the next on-policy batch.

Multi-task learning and conflicting updates.

When a shared model is trained on several sources, gradients can interfere (Caruana, 1997; Ruder, 2017; Sener and Koltun, 2018; Yu et al., 2020). Multi-task RL methods distill shared skills or regularize policies toward a common centroid (Parisotto et al., 2016; Teh et al., 2017; Barreto et al., 2017). Those approaches typically assume a fixed sampling distribution over tasks. In our setting the “tasks” are harnesses that wrap the same underlying ClawGym instances; interference is induced by interface mismatch rather than by disjoint objectives. HarnessBandit does not project or surgically alter gradients. It chooses which harness to roll out so that the observed update is both informative and aligned with other interfaces.

Curriculum learning and data mixing.

Curriculum learning sequences training material by difficulty or progress (Bengio et al., 2009; Graves et al., 2017; Narvekar et al., 2020; Portelas et al., 2020). In language-model pretraining, mixture weights over domains are often tuned offline or by a proxy model (Xie et al., 2023; Albalak et al., 2024). Most such methods do not observe whether an on-policy source currently yields a non-zero advantage or whether its gradient aligns with other sources. A related two-signal bandit has been used to schedule reasoning domains (Yang et al., 2026). We instead allocate training steps across execution harnesses that wrap the same task collection.

Bandit allocation.

Classical bandits allocate pulls under uncertainty (Auer et al., 2002; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020). We use an exponentially weighted value, a visit-dependent bonus, Boltzmann sampling, and a uniform floor; c/nh+1c/\sqrt{n_{h}+1} is an implementation choice rather than a new regret result. The contribution is the execution-harness instantiation and its systems integration.

Gradient similarity and sketches.

Cosine similarity and related kernel alignments are standard probes of whether two updates or representations point in the same direction (Yosinski et al., 2014; Kornblith et al., 2019). Storing one full gradient per harness is impractical at even 2B scale. Linear sketches, including coordinate subsampling and Rademacher projections, preserve inner products in the sense of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma (Johnson and Lindenstrauss, 1984; Achlioptas, 2003; Charikar et al., 2004). HarnessBandit uses a fixed, layer-proportional subsample of the last four transformer blocks so that cosine comparisons remain well-defined across steps without materializing 190M-dimensional buffers.

3 Problem formulation

Tasks and harnesses.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a set of agent tasks. Each task x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} specifies a user query, an initial workspace, and a scalar reward r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1] computed by a programmatic checker after the session ends. A harness h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is an execution interface: it wraps xx with a system prompt, a tool schema, and a control loop, and it induces a trajectory distribution τ∼πθ(⋅∣x,h)\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,h) for a policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. Two harnesses applied to the same xx can produce different tokenizations, different tool-call syntax, and different reward realizations.

Training uses a finite product 𝒟train={(x,h):x∈𝒳train,h∈ℋtrain}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{(x,h):x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{train}},\,h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}\}. Evaluation uses disjoint task collections 𝒳eval\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{eval}} (PinchBench and ClawEval) that are never seen during optimization. PinchBench is executed under OpenClaw, which belongs to ℋtrain\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}; ClawEval uses a native evaluation loop that does not. The intended generalization is therefore across held-out tasks, and, for ClawEval, across interfaces as well.

On-policy update.

We train with group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024). For a prompt (x,h)(x,h) the rollout stack draws GG trajectories, scores them, and forms advantages Ai,tA_{i,t} by subtracting a leave-one-out group baseline. Following Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) we do not divide by the group standard deviation, which avoids exploding updates when intra-group reward variance is near zero. The policy loss at step tt is the usual clipped surrogate plus a KL penalty toward a frozen reference,

ℒt(θ)=𝔼[−min(ρi,tAi,t,clip(ρi,t,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)Ai,t)]+βKLKL(πθ∥πref),\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\min\!\bigl(\rho_{i,t}A_{i,t},\;\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,A_{i,t}\bigr)\right]+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr), (1)

where ρi,t\rho_{i,t} is the importance ratio. Nothing in HarnessBandit depends on this particular surrogate; any on-policy method that yields per-token advantages and a batch gradient can supply the two observations below.

Scheduling objective.

Under the bandit abstraction, the arms are ℋtrain\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}} and one arm is selected at each optimizer step. Because the shared policy changes after every update, arm utilities evolve with θt\theta_{t} rather than following fixed reward distributions. A scheduler is a (possibly randomized) rule σ\sigma that, given history ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, selects ht∈ℋtrainh_{t}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}. The rollout then uses only hth_{t} for every prompt in the batch. We want σ\sigma to trade off two instantaneous properties of hh:

Lh​(θ)\displaystyle L_{h}(\theta) =𝔼[|A||h,θ],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\lvert A\rvert\;\middle|\;h,\,\theta\,\right], (2)
Th​(θ)\displaystyle T_{h}(\theta) =𝔼[1|ℋtrain∖{h}|∑j≠hcos(∇θℒ(h),g¯j)|h,θ],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}\setminus\{h\}\rvert}\sum_{j\neq h}\cos\!\bigl(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(h),\,\bar{g}_{j}\bigr)\;\middle|\;h,\,\theta\right], (3)

where g¯j\bar{g}_{j} is a running estimate of the gradient direction associated with harness jj. LhL_{h} is large when the group contains both successful and unsuccessful trajectories, so the policy gradient is informative. ThT_{h} is large when an update on hh is aligned with the directions previously observed on other harnesses. A scheduler that maximizes only LhL_{h} can concentrate on a harness whose advantages are large but idiosyncratic. A scheduler that maximizes only ThT_{h} can prefer a harness that is well aligned yet currently uninformative (Lh≈0L_{h}\approx 0). HarnessBandit estimates both quantities online and selects hth_{t} to increase a convex combination of their normalized values, subject to exploration.

The quantity we ultimately care about is not LhL_{h} or ThT_{h} themselves, but expected reward on 𝒳eval\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{eval}}. The two signals are instruments: they are cheap to compute from the training step and are intended to allocate a fixed step budget toward updates that are both usable and shareable.

4 Method

HarnessBandit wraps an unchanged GRPO trainer with an online harness scheduler. Figure 1 states the principle: the same tasks are executed through several interfaces, only one interface is active at a step, and the next draw depends on both local learnability and cross-harness transferability. Algorithm 1 gives the per-step procedure. After each update the scheduler records a local learnability signal and a sketched-gradient transferability signal, fuses them after pooled sliding-window min–max normalization, and draws the next harness. The implementation uses a proportional coordinate subsample, per-selected-step signal updates, τ=0.3\tau{=}0.3, and an explicit ε\varepsilon-floor.

4.1 Harness-pure batches

Let ℋtrain={h(1),…,h(H)}\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{h^{(1)},\ldots,h^{(H)}\}. Each harness maintains an independent shuffled pool of the same ClawGym tasks, so harness identity is not confounded with task difficulty. At step tt the scheduler returns one name hth_{t}; every prompt in the rollout batch of size BB is drawn from the pool of hth_{t}. Purity has two consequences. First, the batch gradient is attributable to a single arm, so a cosine against other arms is well-defined. Second, leftover groups produced by oversampling filters can be stashed per harness rather than discarded, which keeps the comparison with a mixed-batch baseline honest on the number of scored trajectories.

4.2 Learnability

After advantages are computed, each trajectory is reduced to a token-masked mean of |Ai,t|\lvert A_{i,t}\rvert. Trajectory means that share a prompt group are averaged, and group means that share a harness are averaged:

Lht=1|𝒢ht|​∑g∈𝒢ht1|𝒯g|​∑τ∈𝒯g|A|¯τ.L_{h_{t}}=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{G}_{h_{t}}\rvert}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{h_{t}}}\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{T}_{g}\rvert}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{g}}\overline{\lvert A\rvert}_{\tau}. (4)

Equal weighting at the group level prevents long trajectories from dominating the signal. If every trajectory in every group of hth_{t} receives the same reward, then Lht≈0L_{h_{t}}\approx 0 and the step is treated as uninformative even if the absolute reward is high.

4.3 Transferability via gradient sketches

Let gh=∇θℒg_{h}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L} be the batch gradient after all microbatches of a pure hh-step have been backwarded and before the optimizer consumes them. We retain only parameters in the last K=4K{=}4 transformer blocks. Embeddings and the output head are excluded: their gradients are dominated by token frequency and therefore track which tasks were sampled rather than how the harness pushes the policy. The selected tensors still contain on the order of 10810^{8} coordinates. A sketch g^h∈ℝd\hat{g}_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with d=65,536d{=}65{,}536 is formed by a fixed random subsample whose per-tensor allocation is proportional to numel⁡(⋅)\mathrm{numel}(\cdot). Proportional allocation keeps each tensor’s contribution to ∥g^h∥22\lVert\hat{g}_{h}\rVert_{2}^{2} scaled by the same constant, so the sketched cosine is not biased by layer shape. Across data-parallel and context-parallel ranks the sketch is summed and renormalized; cosine similarity is scale-invariant, so the subsequent division by world size is only for interpretability.

Each harness stores an exponential moving average EMAj\mathrm{EMA}_{j} of its unit sketch on CPU. After the current sketch is reduced,

Tht=1|J|∑j∈Jcos(g^ht,EMAj),J={j∈ℋtrain:j≠ht,EMAj exists}.T_{h_{t}}=\frac{1}{\lvert J\rvert}\sum_{j\in J}\cos\!\bigl(\hat{g}_{h_{t}},\,\mathrm{EMA}_{j}\bigr),\qquad J=\{j\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}:j\neq h_{t},\;\mathrm{EMA}_{j}\text{ exists}\}. (5)

If JJ is empty—as it is on the first visit to each arm—ThtT_{h_{t}} is left undefined and the score below falls back to learnability alone. The EMA is then updated with rate η=0.3\eta{=}0.3.

4.4 Normalization, fusion, and value update

LhL_{h} and ThT_{h} have different units. Each is min–max normalized over a sliding window of the last W=32W{=}32 raw observations, pooled across harnesses:

L~h=clip⁡(Lh−min⁡𝒲Lmax⁡𝒲L−min⁡𝒲L, 0,1),\tilde{L}_{h}=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{L_{h}-\min\mathcal{W}_{L}}{\max\mathcal{W}_{L}-\min\mathcal{W}_{L}},\,0,1\right), (6)

and likewise for T~h\tilde{T}_{h}. Per-arm windows would erase the between-arm contrasts that the bandit needs. If a window contains fewer than two values, the normalized coordinate is set to 1/21/2. The instantaneous score is

Sh={α​L~h+(1−α)​T~hif both are defined,L~h​ or ​T~hif only one is defined.S_{h}=\begin{cases}\alpha\,\tilde{L}_{h}+(1-\alpha)\,\tilde{T}_{h}&\text{if both are defined,}\\[2.0pt] \tilde{L}_{h}\text{ or }\tilde{T}_{h}&\text{if only one is defined.}\end{cases} (7)

We use α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5. The per-arm value is an EMA, Qh←(1−β)​Qh+β​ShQ_{h}\leftarrow(1-\beta)Q_{h}+\beta S_{h} with β=0.3\beta{=}0.3. An unvisited arm is assigned maxj⁡Qj\max_{j}Q_{j} at selection time so that softmax cannot starve it before the first observation.

4.5 Sampling

The quantity that is ranked is Uh=Qh+c/nh+1U_{h}=Q_{h}+c/\sqrt{n_{h}+1} with c=0.2c{=}0.2. The sampling distribution is

ph=(1−ε)​softmax​(U/τ)h+ε/H,τ=0.3,ε=0.15.p_{h}=(1-\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{softmax}(U/\tau)_{h}+\varepsilon/H,\qquad\tau{=}0.3,\;\varepsilon{=}0.15. (8)

The temperature τ\tau controls how sharply the curriculum concentrates; the floor ε\varepsilon guarantees a minimum rate that does not depend on nhn_{h}. The bonus c/nh+1c/\sqrt{n_{h}+1} is the term that actually prefers under-sampled arms. Because the bonus does not grow with tt (unlike UCB1’s ln⁡t/n\sqrt{\ln t/n}), an arm that stops being drawn keeps a frozen bonus and cannot rescue itself. That is why ε\varepsilon and cc are not interchangeable.

The first Wup=30W_{\mathrm{up}}{=}30 steps ignore pp and cycle through ℋtrain\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}} in round-robin order, so every arm has at least five observations before the bandit takes over.

4.6 Complexity

Relative to an existing GRPO step, the extra work is (i) a gather of dd gradient coordinates on KK layers, (ii) an all-reduce of a dd-vector, and (iii) O⁡(H​d)O(Hd) cosine evaluations. With d=65,536d{=}65{,}536 and H=6H{=}6, the EMA store occupies a few megabytes rather than several gigabytes. The policy loss, rollout, and reward evaluation are unchanged. HarnessBandit is therefore a constant-factor add-on to an existing GRPO run, not a second trainer.

5 Experiments

5.1 Training setup

Data.

Training uses 2,000 ClawGym tasks (RUC-AIBOX, 2025). Each task directory contains a user query, optional workspace files, and a reward.sh checker that prints a scalar in [0,1][0,1]. We form a Cartesian product with six training harnesses—Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Pi, OpenClaw, and Codex—yielding 12,000 prompt rows. Every method therefore sees the same task universe; harness identity is not confounded with difficulty.

Policy and optimizer.

The policy is Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026), trained with Polar (Xu et al., 2026) and slime/Megatron GRPO (Shoeybi et al., 2019) on four GPUs. We use Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) (leave-one-out baseline, no standard-deviation normalization), Adam at 10−610^{-6} with a constant schedule, KL coefficient 0.050.05, rollout batch size B=8B{=}8, G=8G{=}8 samples per prompt, and 150 optimizer steps. Dynamic sampling drops groups with zero reward standard deviation. Context parallelism is 4 and the maximum response length is 8,192 tokens.

HarnessBandit hyperparameters.

Unless noted: α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, β=0.3\beta{=}0.3, τ=0.3\tau{=}0.3, c=0.2c{=}0.2, ε=0.15\varepsilon{=}0.15, warmup 3030 steps, window 3232, sketch dimension 65,53665{,}536, last K=4K{=}4 layers, sketch EMA 0.30.3.

Comparisons.

All trained methods share the optimizer, data product, step budget, and hardware.

  • •

    HarnessBandit: one harness per batch, selected as in Section 4.

  • •

    Mixed (6 harnesses): the same 12,000-row file with a global shuffle, so a batch of eight prompts typically mixes several harnesses. No bandit and no gradient sketch.

  • •

    Mixed (OpenClaw+Codex): the same mixed loader restricted to two harnesses. This tests whether a smaller interface set is sufficient.

  • •

    Qwen3.5-2B (base): the untuned checkpoint, evaluated with the same serving stack.

5.2 Evaluation protocol

Held-out evaluation uses two independent benchmarks. Both use tasks disjoint from ClawGym. They differ in whether the evaluation interface belongs to ℋtrain\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}.

PinchBench.

We report official-suite results on 147 tasks, one run per task, in the official OpenClaw Docker environment (PinchBench, 2026). OpenClaw is one of the six training harnesses, so this suite is out-of-distribution in tasks and in-distribution in interface. The metric is the mean automated task score in [0,1][0,1].

ClawEval.

We follow the official protocol on the general split (161 tasks) with N=3N{=}3 independent trials (Claw-Eval Team, 2026). Execution uses ClawEval’s own think–act–observe loop and per-task tool schemas, not any member of ℋtrain\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{train}}. The suite is therefore out-of-distribution in both tasks and interface. Pass3 is the fraction of tasks that pass on all three trials; pass@3 is the fraction that pass on at least one trial; the average score is the mean of the 161 per-task scores.

5.3 Results

Table 1 summarizes the two benchmarks. On PinchBench (held-out tasks, OpenClaw), HarnessBandit records 0.5060.506, a +1.3+1.3 point edge over the two-harness OpenClaw–Codex mixture (0.4930.493) and a +17.6+17.6 point gap over both the six-harness mixture (0.3310.331) and the untuned base model (0.3300.330). The six-harness mixed-batch run is essentially tied with the base model, so shuffling all six interfaces into mixed batches does not improve the official mean; restricting the mixed loader to OpenClaw and Codex accounts for nearly all of the trained-policy gain on this suite.

On ClawEval (held-out tasks, native loop) the ranking depends on the metric. Pass3 ties HarnessBandit with the untuned base model at 43/16143/161 (26.7%26.7\%) and places both mixed schedules below the base model (3535 and 3232 tasks). Pass@3 and mean score separate the checkpoints: HarnessBandit reaches 67/16167/161 (41.6%41.6\%) and 0.5560.556, against 62/16162/161 (38.5%38.5\%) / 0.5100.510 for the six-harness mixture, 58/16158/161 (36.0%36.0\%) / 0.5340.534 for the base model, and 48/16148/161 (29.8%29.8\%) / 0.4900.490 for the two-harness mixture. Thus both static mixtures underperform the base model on Pass3 and on mean score; only HarnessBandit matches the base model on the strict official criterion and exceeds it on pass@3 and average score. PinchBench category means (Appendix B) are highest for HarnessBandit on analysis, log analysis, productivity, research, skills, writing, and integrations. The two-harness mixture is higher on coding, CSV analysis, meeting analysis, and memory. The six-harness mixture wins no category and scores zero on writing.

5.4 Bandit behavior

Figure C.1 (Appendix C) shows the induced schedule. After warmup the mass is non-uniform: OpenClaw, Pi, and OpenCode end near p=0.20,0.20,0.18p=0.20,0.20,0.18, whereas Qwen Code and Codex end near 0.13,0.140.13,0.14. Final visit counts range from 2121 to 3232, a mild reallocation rather than collapse.

Figure 2 shows that the two signals give different rankings. Pi has the highest mean normalized learnability (0.750.75) but only mid-range transferability (0.490.49); OpenCode is high on both (0.62,0.600.62,0.60); OpenClaw’s transferability (0.590.59) exceeds its learnability (0.550.55); Qwen Code is lower on transferability (0.370.37) than learnability (0.530.53). Thus transferability is not a monotone transformation of learnability in this run. Marker area reflects mean sampling probability php_{h}, which is largest for OpenCode (0.210.21) and OpenClaw (0.180.18).

Appendix E plots directed pairwise gradient cosines. They mostly fluctuate around zero, with both positive and negative intervals and no uniformly beneficial source harness. This fine-grained geometry explains why the scalar transferability state changes over time.

6 Conclusion

Multi-harness agentic RL requires a decision that GRPO does not make: which interface should generate the next on-policy batch. We argued that the decision should depend on learnability of the current update and transferability of that update across harnesses. HarnessBandit estimates both from GRPO advantages and sketched last-layer gradients, fuses them after shared-window normalization, and samples a harness-pure batch with a UCB-softmax rule.

After 150 GRPO steps on a ClawGym ×\times six-harness product, a Qwen3.5-2B policy trained with HarnessBandit records a higher official PinchBench mean than both mixed schedules (held-out tasks, in-distribution OpenClaw). On ClawEval (held-out tasks and harness) it matches the untuned base model on Pass3 (26.7%26.7\%) while improving pass@3 and mean score, and it exceeds both mixtures on all three ClawEval metrics. The induced schedule is a mild reweighting, not a collapse to one harness.

Appendix A Hyperparameters

Table A.1 lists the GRPO and scheduler settings shared by every trained method. The optimizer, batch size, sample count, step budget, and hardware are matched so that Table 1 isolates harness allocation. The bandit knobs (α,β,τ,c,ε\alpha,\beta,\tau,c,\varepsilon, warmup, window, sketch) are the values used for the reported HarnessBandit run; mixed-batch baselines ignore them.

Appendix B PinchBench category means

Table B.1 breaks the official PinchBench mean into the suite’s task categories. Cell sizes are identical across methods, so differences are not an artifact of a different task mix. HarnessBandit is highest on analysis, integrations, log analysis, productivity, research, skills, and writing. The two-harness OpenClaw–Codex mixture is higher on coding, CSV analysis, meeting analysis, and memory—categories that align with those two interfaces. The six-harness mixture wins no category; its writing cell is exactly zero, which we treat as a recorded score rather than evidence that the mixture cannot write. The overall row reproduces Table 1.

Appendix C Bandit schedule

Figure C.1 shows the sampling distribution php_{h} and the visit counts nhn_{h} on the reported run. The first 30 steps are a round-robin warmup, so every harness is observed before softmax takes over. After that line the mass is non-uniform but stays away from a one-arm collapse: OpenClaw, Pi, and OpenCode receive more probability, while Qwen Code and Codex remain above the ε\varepsilon-floor. Visit counts at the end of training span 21–32 (Appendix F), which is a mild reallocation of a 150-step budget.

Appendix D Raw online signals

Figure D.1 plots the un-normalized observations that later become L~h\tilde{L}_{h} and T~h\tilde{T}_{h}. Learnability LhL_{h} is a mean absolute advantage and stays clearly positive; transferability ThT_{h} is an average cosine and fluctuates in a narrow band around zero. The two traces therefore live in different units, which is why Section 4.4 applies a shared sliding-window min–max before fusion. Rankings also differ: a harness can look learnable on the left panel while sitting near the bottom of the right panel. Figure 2 in the main text shows the same run after normalization.

Appendix E Pairwise gradient geometry

The scalar ThtT_{h_{t}} averages the current sketch against every other harness EMA. Figure E.1 unrolls that average into directed pairs. Each panel fixes the source harness; each line is the cosine from that source’s current sketch to one peer EMA. The traces move through both positive and negative intervals and do not identify a source that is aligned with all peers at all times. That geometry is why the fused transferability state in Figure 2 evolves rather than locking onto a single “helpful” interface.

Appendix F Final HarnessBandit state

These are the terminal php_{h} and nhn_{h} of Figure C.1, recorded after the last optimizer step. Sampling probabilities are OpenClaw 0.2040.204, Pi 0.1970.197, OpenCode 0.1840.184, Gemini CLI 0.1510.151, Codex 0.1370.137, Qwen Code 0.1270.127. Visit counts are OpenCode 3232, OpenClaw 2626, Qwen Code 2424, Codex 2424, Gemini CLI 2121, Pi 2121 (148 observations after warmup). Uniform allocation over six arms would give ph=1/6≈0.167p_{h}=1/6\approx 0.167 and about 25 visits each; the observed schedule is a tilt toward OpenClaw, Pi, and OpenCode, not a collapse to one arm. Pi’s visit count is low relative to its final php_{h} because probability mass arrived late.
